q: What is the project life cycle?
options: The set of tools used to track a project's budget
The series of phases a project goes through from inception to completion within time, cost, and quality constraints
The ongoing, repetitive work that keeps an organization running
The document that formally authorizes a project
explanation: The project life cycle is the series of phases from inception to completion, kept within time, cost, and quality constraints. Ongoing repetitive work is operations, and the authorizing document is the Project Charter.

q: Which document formally authorizes a project and states its purpose, objectives, high-level requirements, and major stakeholders?
options: Project Management Plan
Stakeholder Register
Final Project Report
Project Charter
explanation: The Project Charter formally authorizes the project. The Project Management Plan explains how the project is carried out, the Stakeholder Register lists stakeholders, and the Final Project Report is made at Closing.

q: What is a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)?
options: A hierarchical breakdown of the project scope into smaller, manageable sections
A list of stakeholders with their roles, interests, and influence
A log of risks and issues found during the project
A report comparing actual progress against the baseline
explanation: A WBS decomposes the scope into manageable sections. The stakeholder list is the Stakeholder Register, risks go in the Risk and Issue Log, and progress against the baseline is a Status Report.

q: What does a Stakeholder Register record?
options: The approved scope, schedule, and cost
The final outcomes and achievements of the project
The roles, interests, and influence of the people involved in the project
Every change request and whether it was approved
explanation: The Stakeholder Register documents stakeholders' roles, interests, and influence. Approved scope, schedule, and cost are baselines; final outcomes go in closure documentation.

q: In project management, what is a baseline?
options: The first meeting with the whole project team
The approved original plan for scope, schedule, and cost that actual progress is measured against
A measurable target used to judge team performance
The minimum quality a deliverable must reach before handover
explanation: A baseline is the approved reference plan for scope, schedule, and cost. The first team meeting is the kickoff meeting, and measurable performance targets are KPIs.

q: Who is the sponsor of a project?
options: The person who starts and supports the project, usually a senior executive
The team member who inspects the deliverables
The client who receives the final deliverable at Closing
The person who writes the Lessons Learned Document
explanation: The sponsor initiates and supports the project and is usually a senior executive. The project manager gathers the scope, timeline, and business justification from the sponsor during Initiating.

q: What is a change request?
options: A report on how the work is progressing
A request from the sponsor to start a new project
A review of wins and losses at the end of the project
A formal request to change the project that is evaluated and then approved or rejected
explanation: A change request is a formal request to change the project, evaluated and then approved or rejected. Progress reports are Performance Reports, and the end review is part of Closing.

q: What are Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) used for in the Monitoring and Controlling phase?
options: Breaking the scope into smaller sections
Formally authorizing the project
Measuring whether the team and project are performing against goals
Listing the people affected by the project
explanation: Monitoring and Controlling tracks team performance against KPIs and goals. Breaking scope down is the WBS, authorizing is the Project Charter, and listing people is the Stakeholder Register.

q: Within which three constraints does the project life cycle keep a project?
options: Time, cost, and quality
Scope, risk, and communication
People, equipment, and money
Vision, goals, and objectives
explanation: The life cycle runs from inception to completion within time, cost, and quality constraints. People, equipment, and money are resource types; vision, goals, and objectives are defined in Initiation.

q: Which phase is described as the most extensive phase of the project life cycle?
options: Executing
Planning
Controlling and Monitoring
Initiating
explanation: Planning is the most extensive phase because it decides how the project will be carried out, managed, and controlled across scope, time, cost, quality, risk, resources, and communication. Executing is action-oriented but is not called the most extensive.

q: Which phase runs at the same time as Executing?
options: Planning
Initiating
Closing
Controlling and Monitoring
explanation: Controlling and Monitoring runs alongside Executing to keep time, scope, and budget on track. Planning can overlap with Executing, but the phase defined as running concurrently with it is Controlling and Monitoring.

q: Which set lists the three outputs of the Planning phase?
options: Project Charter, Stakeholder Register, Project Management Plan
Status Reports, Updated Project Plans, Risk and Issue Logs
Project Management Plan, Work Breakdown Structure, Baseline Plans
Project Deliverables, Performance Reports, Change Requests
explanation: Planning outputs the Project Management Plan, the WBS, and baselines for scope, schedule, and cost. The Charter and Register come from Initiating, Status Reports from Monitoring and Controlling, and Deliverables from Executing.

q: Which set lists the three outputs of the Closing phase?
options: Final Project Report, Lessons Learned Document, Project Closure Documents
Project Deliverables, Performance Reports, Change Requests
Status Reports, Updated Project Plans, Risk and Issue Logs
Project Charter, Stakeholder Register, Baseline Plans
explanation: Closing produces the Final Project Report, the Lessons Learned Document, and Project Closure Documents. The other sets belong to Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, and a mix of Initiating and Planning.

q: What is the correct order of the five phases of the project life cycle?
options: Planning, Initiating, Executing, Closing, Monitoring and Controlling
Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, Closing
Initiating, Executing, Planning, Monitoring and Controlling, Closing
Initiating, Planning, Monitoring and Controlling, Closing, Executing
explanation: The phases are Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, then Closing. A project must be authorized before it is planned, and planned before the work is executed.

q: In the Initiating phase, what comes first before the project can be planned?
options: Holding the kickoff meeting, then creating the WBS
Building the baselines, then identifying stakeholders
Getting the project details from the sponsor, then developing the Project Charter
Writing performance reports, then approving change requests
explanation: The project manager first gathers scope, timelines, and justification from the sponsor, then develops the Charter that formally authorizes the project. The kickoff, WBS, and baselines come in Planning.

q: What is the correct order of these outputs as a project moves through its life cycle: Status Report, Project Charter, Lessons Learned Document, Work Breakdown Structure?
options: Work Breakdown Structure, Project Charter, Status Report, Lessons Learned Document
Project Charter, Status Report, Work Breakdown Structure, Lessons Learned Document
Project Charter, Work Breakdown Structure, Lessons Learned Document, Status Report
Project Charter, Work Breakdown Structure, Status Report, Lessons Learned Document
explanation: Charter (Initiating), WBS (Planning), Status Report (Monitoring and Controlling), Lessons Learned (Closing). Putting the WBS before the Charter plans a project that has not been authorized.

q: How does a change request move through the life cycle?
options: It is raised during Executing, then reviewed and approved or rejected through change control in Monitoring and Controlling
It is approved in Initiating, then raised in Planning
It is raised in Closing, then recorded in the Lessons Learned Document
It is reviewed in Planning, then raised during Executing
explanation: Change requests are an output of Executing, and change control in Monitoring and Controlling decides whether to approve or reject them. A request must exist before it can be reviewed.

q: Which pairing of an output and its phase is mismatched?
options: Stakeholder Register: Initiating
Work Breakdown Structure: Executing
Risk and Issue Logs: Controlling and Monitoring
Final Project Report: Closing
explanation: The WBS is a Planning output, not an Executing output. The other three pairs are correct.

q: Which statement about Quality Assurance and Quality Control is NOT true?
options: Quality Assurance is an activity of the Executing phase
Quality Control is an activity of the Monitoring and Controlling phase
Quality Control inspects the deliverables
Quality Assurance inspects the finished deliverables, while Quality Control monitors the processes
explanation: This reverses them. Quality Assurance monitors the processes during Executing; Quality Control inspects the deliverables during Monitoring and Controlling.

q: Which statement about the phases of a project is NOT true?
options: Phases are often sequential but can overlap
Planning and Executing can overlap as details are refined
Each phase must be fully finished before the next one can begin
Executing and Monitoring and Controlling run at the same time
explanation: The phases are often sequential but can overlap, so they do not each have to be fully finished first. Executing and Monitoring and Controlling run together, and Planning and Executing can overlap.

q: Which pairing of an activity and its phase is mismatched?
options: Stakeholder Feedback: Initiating
Team Development: Executing
Change Control: Controlling and Monitoring
Develop Project Charter: Initiating
explanation: Stakeholder Feedback is a Closing activity. Identify Stakeholders is the Initiating activity, which is a different task. The other three pairs are correct.

q: A project manager meets the senior executive who proposed a new mobile app to learn the scope, the expected timeline, and why the app is worth building. Which phase is this?
options: Planning
Initiating
Executing
Closing
explanation: Gathering the scope, timeline, and business justification from the sponsor happens in Initiating, before the Charter is made. Planning starts once the project is authorized.

q: Midway through building a library system, the manager compares money spent so far against the approved budget and finds the project 10 percent over. Which output records this comparison?
options: Performance Report
Project Charter
Final Project Report
Status Report
explanation: Comparing progress against the baseline produces a Status Report in Monitoring and Controlling. A Performance Report (Executing) shows how work is progressing but is not the baseline comparison, and the Final Project Report is made at Closing.

q: A team takes the scope 'campus event website', splits it into home page, registration, and gallery, then splits registration into form, database, and confirmation email. What are they creating, and in which phase?
options: A Stakeholder Register in Initiating
A Change Request in Executing
A Work Breakdown Structure in Planning
A Status Report in Monitoring and Controlling
explanation: Breaking scope into smaller levels (website, then sections, then tasks) is a hierarchical decomposition, which is a WBS, a Planning output.

q: A student writes: 'Step 1, Initiating: create the Project Charter. Step 2, Planning: create the WBS and baselines. Step 3, Executing: write the Lessons Learned Document. Step 4, Closing: hand over the final deliverables.' Which step is wrong?
options: Step 3, because the Lessons Learned Document is a Closing output
Step 1, because the Charter is made in Planning
Step 2, because baselines are made in Monitoring and Controlling
Step 4, because handover happens in Executing
explanation: Lessons Learned is written in Closing, after the project's results are known. The Charter is an Initiating output, baselines are Planning outputs, and handover is a Closing activity, so Steps 1, 2, and 4 are right.

q: A reviewer claims: 'Testers inspecting the finished login module for bugs is Quality Assurance, so it belongs to the Executing phase.' What is the error?
options: Inspecting a module is Change Control, which belongs to Planning
Inspecting finished deliverables is Quality Control, which belongs to Monitoring and Controlling
Testing belongs to Closing because the module is finished
There is no error; Quality Assurance inspects deliverables
explanation: Inspecting deliverables is Quality Control in Monitoring and Controlling. Quality Assurance monitors processes during Executing. Change Control decides on change requests and is not in Planning.

q: During development of a payroll app, the HR head asks to add a tax report feature. The manager then reviews the extra cost and approves it, and the plan is revised. Which three items are produced or used, in order?
options: Change Request, Change Control, Updated Project Plans
Project Charter, Stakeholder Register, Final Project Report
Status Report, Lessons Learned Document, Baseline Plans
Work Breakdown Structure, Performance Report, Project Closure Documents
explanation: The HR head's request is a Change Request (Executing), the manager's review is Change Control, and the revised plan is an Updated Project Plan (both Monitoring and Controlling).

q: A project manager is handed three tasks: inspect the finished deliverables, record what went well and badly, and get the client's sign-off. Which phases do these belong to, in that order?
options: Executing, Closing, Initiating
Planning, Executing, Closing
Monitoring and Controlling, Executing, Closing
Monitoring and Controlling, Closing, Closing
explanation: Inspecting deliverables is Quality Control (Monitoring and Controlling). Recording lessons learned and the final handover with client sign-off are both Closing activities.

q: A barangay project to install solar streetlights has these events: (a) the team lists residents, the council, and the contractor with their interests; (b) workers install the poles; (c) the council confirms the lights work and the project is archived. Which outputs match (a), (b), and (c)?
options: Project Charter, Performance Report, Status Report
Stakeholder Register, Project Deliverables, Project Closure Documents
Stakeholder Register, Change Requests, Lessons Learned Document
Work Breakdown Structure, Project Deliverables, Final Project Report
explanation: Listing stakeholders with their interests is the Stakeholder Register (Initiating); the installed poles are deliverables (Executing); confirming completion so the project can be archived is the Project Closure Documents (Closing).

q: Which of these activities belongs to the Executing phase?
options: Developing the Project Charter
Setting the schedule's milestones and dependencies
Allocating people and equipment to tasks and developing the team
Reflecting on wins and losses
explanation: Resource Allocation and Team Development are Executing activities. The Charter is Initiating, milestones and dependencies are time planning, and reflecting on wins and losses is Closing.
